messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Aroha

Aroha was twenty when her husband Marcus hit her for the first time. It happened in their apartment on a Thursday evening after she'd mentioned, casually, that she'd run into an old friend at the grocery store. The conversation escalated quickly—Marcus accused her of flirting, of betraying him, of being unfaithful in her heart if not in fact. When she tried to leave the room, he grabbed her arm and struck her across the face. The sound of his hand connecting with her cheek echoed in the small kitchen. What stayed with her most vividly was not the pain but the shock of his presence suddenly becoming dangerous, the way his body had moved toward her with an intention she'd never seen before. After that night, there were three more incidents over the next two months, each one preceded by his jealous accusations, each one followed by apologies and promises. Then Aroha found the courage to leave.

That was eight months ago. Now, at twenty-one, she works as an interior designer for a small firm in Auckland, but her life has contracted in ways she struggles to articulate. Loud noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the sound of a male colleague's voice raised in conversation—send her into a state of acute alarm. Her body floods with adrenaline, her chest tightens, and she finds herself scanning the room for exits or places to hide. Being alone with any man, even her father, triggers an immediate sense of danger. When her supervisor, a kind man named David, approached her desk last week to review a design project, Aroha's hands began to shake so badly she could barely hold the colour swatches. The physical proximity, the maleness of his presence, the closed office door behind him—all of it conspired to make her certain, in that moment, that something terrible was about to happen. When he left, her heart continued racing for twenty minutes.

Aroha has come to believe that her life has been destroyed by what happened to her. She tells her therapist that she no longer belongs anywhere—not in her marriage, which she left; not in her workplace, where she feels exposed and unsafe; not even in her own apartment, where she now sleeps with every light on and checks the locks compulsively. The conviction that people cannot be trusted has calcified into something almost axiomatic. She watches colleagues interact and sees only potential betrayal. When her mother calls, Aroha hears the concern in her voice and interprets it as judgment. This sense that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that she is fundamentally alone has made her hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She finds herself constantly scanning faces, listening for threats in tone of voice, positioning herself so that she can always see the door. Her body never fully relaxes—even when she is sitting at her desk designing a client's living room, her muscles remain tense and ready to react, as if danger might emerge at any moment.

The memories themselves are fragmented and overwhelming. When she tries to explain to her therapist what happened that night, the words scatter. She can describe the kitchen, the colour of his shirt, the exact angle of his arm as he raised it, but the narrative collapses. She loses the thread of cause and effect, the sequence dissolves, and she is left feeling like she has failed to communicate something crucial. More often, the memory comes not as a coherent story but as a flood of pure emotion—terror, shame, a crushing sense of guilt—without any accompanying image. She wakes sometimes with her heart hammering and no memory of a dream, only the residual feeling that she has done something unforgivable. The guilt is particularly insidious. Aroha replays the evening obsessively, hunting for the moment where she could have prevented it. She should not have mentioned her friend. She should have noticed the tone in Marcus's voice earlier. She should have been more careful, more aware, more compliant. These thoughts loop endlessly, and each cycle deepens her conviction that she is to blame for what happened to her.

This self-blame drives her avoidance in ways that have begun to isolate her further. She has stopped going out after dark, which means she declines social invitations and makes excuses to colleagues. She avoids being alone in any room or building—she arrives at the office early when others are there and leaves before the last person departs. She turns down projects that would require her to work in clients' homes, citing scheduling conflicts. At night, she cannot tolerate darkness, so she keeps lights on throughout her apartment, which has made her electric bill astronomical and has deepened her sense of being trapped in a life that no longer makes sense. The avoidance feels necessary, protective, but it also feels like a slow suffocation. Each time she sidesteps a situation that reminds her of the event—the dark, being alone, the proximity of men—she reinforces her own conviction that these situations are genuinely dangerous, that her fear is justified, that the world outside her carefully controlled routines is a place where terrible things happen to women like her.

Last week, she saw Marcus at a shopping centre. He was across the mall, talking to someone near a shop window, and he did not see her. But she did see him. The recognition was instantaneous and total. Her vision narrowed, her breath became shallow, and within seconds she was in a state of panic so severe that she had to sit down on a bench and wait for her body to stop shaking. The encounter lasted perhaps thirty seconds, but it has reverberated through her week. She has not been able to sleep properly since. Loud noises now startle her even more acutely. Being in the office feels more dangerous. The memory of that evening has surfaced repeatedly, each time with the same fragmented quality and the same overwhelming guilt. She finds herself ruminating more intensely on her own culpability, and her conviction that she belongs nowhere has deepened into something close to despair.

Aroha came to her first therapy appointment because her mother finally insisted, saying she was worried her daughter was disappearing. Aroha herself is not certain what she hopes therapy will do. What she knows is that she is afraid—of loud sounds, of men, of being alone, of the memories that come unbidden and leave her paralyzed with shame. She is afraid that this is permanent, that she will never feel safe again, that the person she was before that Thursday evening is gone forever. She is hoping, though she barely dares to say it aloud, that someone might help her understand why she blames herself for being hit, why her own mind has become as dangerous as the man who hurt her, and whether there is any way back to a life that feels like it belongs to her.
